title: False Memory: You Remember Things That Never Happened (Lost in the Mall Study)
description:
False memories are real: your brain doesn't replay memories like a video, it rebuilds them every time you recall them, and it can rebuild things that never happened.

The famous experiment:
- In 1995, psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell gave 24 people four short stories about their childhood, written with help from their relatives.
- Three were true. One was invented: getting lost in a shopping mall around age five.
- After the interviews, about 1 in 4 (6 of 24) remembered the fake event, fully or partly.
- A 2023 replication with 123 people found 35%. Across later memory-implant studies, rates often land between 30% and 50%.

This is why eyewitness memory can be confident and still wrong. Which childhood memory are you most sure about?

Sources:
- University College Cork (2023), replication of the Lost in the Mall study: https://cora.ucc.ie/server/api/core/bitstreams/075c236a-356f-4694-94c5-9500b6c148d3/content
- Wellcome Collection, Lost in the mall and other false memories: https://wellcomecollection.org/articles/XQze2hIAAGYP8ckl
- Association for Psychological Science, Grand illusions of memory (Loftus): https://www.psychologicalscience.org/observer/grand-illusions-of-memory-keynote-address-showcases-evidence-of-false-memories

questions.q: Can you remember something that never happened?
questions.a: Yes. Memory is reconstructive: each time you recall an event, the brain rebuilds it, and suggestion can add details or whole events that never happened.

questions.q: What was the Lost in the Mall experiment?
questions.a: In 1995 Elizabeth Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell gave 24 adults four childhood stories, one of them invented (getting lost in a shopping mall). About 25% came to remember the invented one.
A 2023 replication found 35% of participants formed a false memory of the mall event, and later implantation studies often report rates between 30% and 50%.
